claims.text: Some BCC refractory high-entropy alloys possess exceptional strength and strength retention at high temperatures.
Across refractory high-entropy alloys, high-temperature mechanical strength and thermoelastic response are primarily controlled by edge dislocations rather than screw dislocations.
NbTaTiV is a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy in which high-temperature strength is attributable to edge dislocations.
CrMoNbV is a high-strength, low-density BCC refractory high-entropy alloy in which high-temperature strength is attributable to edge dislocations.
Plastic flow in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys is generally controlled by screw dislocations.
A targeted pre-straining and annealing treatment can selectively increase both the density and mobility of edge dislocations.
In-situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM can monitor edge-versus-screw dislocation character during deformation.
Edge-dislocation density and mobility mediate local lattice distortions and their interactions with compositional complexity.
Increasing the presence of edge dislocations increases the activation-energy barrier for slip.
The increased slip barrier caused by edge dislocations retards plastic flow and raises yield strength.
Edge dislocations contribute to elevated-temperature strength retention in NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV.
Edge dislocations alter the elastic lattice response under thermal stress and thereby influence thermoelastic moduli.
Samples treated to increase edge-dislocation density will have higher yield strength than standard-processed reference samples.
Samples treated to increase edge-dislocation density will retain more strength at high temperature than standard-processed reference samples.
Samples treated to increase edge-dislocation density will exhibit a changed thermoelastic modulus relative to reference samples.
Standard processing of the proposed reference alloys produces a dislocation population dominated by screw dislocations.
The proposed edge-dislocation mechanism is most influential above 50% of the alloy melting temperature.
The edge-dislocation mechanism is principally applicable to BCC refractory high-entropy alloys at high temperature.
Phase transformations, extremely high strain rates, or dominance by other microstructural factors can make the edge-dislocation effect less discernible.
The quantitative contribution of edge-dislocation density may vary across refractory high-entropy-alloy compositions and processing histories.
